passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of varying doses of a new cognitive enhancer on reaction time in healthy adults. One hundred twenty participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: Control (no drug), Low Dose (10 mg), Medium Dose (20 mg), and High Dose (30 mg). Each participant performed a computerized reaction time task, and the mean response time (in seconds) along with the standard deviation and sample size (N) were recorded. The data suggested a dose‑dependent improvement, with the High Dose group showing the fastest responses. The study aimed to identify the optimal dose that maximizes benefit while minimizing side effects. The researchers also collected safety data, but the primary outcome was reaction time. The findings could inform dosage recommendations for clinical use and guide future trials on cognitive enhancement.
stem: Which group had the lowest mean reaction time?
explanation: The table shows the mean reaction times for each group. The High Dose group had the lowest mean (10.2 s), indicating the fastest responses.
trap: Students may mistakenly pick Low Dose because it is the first dose listed or because they assume a linear trend.

stem: Which experimental design would best determine the dose‑response relationship?
explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is the gold standard for establishing causal dose‑response effects because it controls for confounding variables and assigns participants to dose groups randomly.
trap: Students may choose an observational study because it is easier to conduct, overlooking the importance of randomization for causal inference.

stem: What is the overall mean reaction time across all groups?
explanation: Because each group has the same sample size (N=30), the overall mean is simply the average of the four group means: (12.5+11.8+11.0+10.2)/4 = 45.5/4 = 11.375 s ≈ 11.4 s.
trap: Picking 13.0 s or 14.0 s, which lie above even the control mean (12.5 s); an overall mean must fall between the lowest and highest group means.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a valid reason to use the mean as a measure of central tendency?

options.C: When data are roughly symmetric with no extreme outliers
options.D: When data are interval or ratio level

explanation: The mean is appropriate for roughly symmetric, normally distributed data without extreme outliers (options A and C) and for interval or ratio scales (option D). It is not a good choice when data are heavily skewed (option B) because the mean is pulled toward the tail.
trap: Students often think the mean is always appropriate, ignoring that skewness and outliers can distort it.

stem: Which analysis is most appropriate for testing whether mean reaction time differs among the four dose groups?

options.D: Pearson correlation between age and reaction time

explanation: Comparing the means of more than two independent groups on a continuous outcome calls for a one-way ANOVA (followed by post hoc tests); repeated t-tests would inflate the Type I error rate.
trap: A paired t-test applies to two related measurements, not four independent groups.
